Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code, you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismat.content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. model:vllm|title:introducing kinference.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . model:vllm|title:migrating vllm to the l.content_excerpt: vLLM relies heavily on PyTorch, with frequent calls to LibTorch in its C++ backend. As a result, changes to LibTorch’s binary interface may require vLLM to be rebuilt and relinked, even when the APIs remain unchanged. What if we could update LibTorch without rebuilding vLLM? That’s where the LibTorch Stable ABI comes in. With a LibTorch Stable ABI, updating LibTorch does not require rebuilding or updating vLLM in order to keep using it. Instead, we could swap out the torch wheel and import it directly into our vLLM package. As of v0.33.0, vLLM publishes LibTorch ABI Stable CUDA wheels. Left: Unstable ABI—new torch requires vLLM to rebuild. Right: Stable ABI—vLLM can import new torch directly. Note: Compatibility between vLLM and PyTorch still depends on other factors, including Python APIs, GPU-related requirements (such as the minimum supported CUDA version), and third-party dependencies. The LibTorch Stable ABI addresses binary compatibility but does not eliminate these other constraints. An application binary interface (ABI) defines how compiled code interacts with a library: how functions are called, data is laid out, and symbols are named. Even if an API looks the same in source code, an ABI change can force extensions to rebuild. A stable ABI preserves a supported set of binary interfaces across compatible versions, so extensions that use them can keep working without a rebuild. PyTorch's LibTorch Stable ABI has three layers: a stable C shim exposing selected LibTorch APIs, C++ wrappers that make the shim easier to use, and headeronly utilities in torch::headeronly that do not link against libtorch.so . Before the Stable ABI, a new PyTorch release could require a vLLM rebuild, delaying support for the new version and its features. With the Stable ABI, the same vLLM wheel can work across compatible PyTorch releases, letting users upgrade sooner and reducing rebuilds for package distributors. For developers, this means you can update and rebuild PyTorch, then test those changes in vLLM without rebuilding vLLM. Left: vLLM needs to change as LibTorch changes. Right: vLLM can change independent of LibTorch. The LibTorch Stable ABI is a limited subset of all of LibTorch. While many common ops are already supported through the C shim and through the higher level C++ convenience wrappers, not all are. story|title:accelerate gpu training on u.content_excerpt: GPUs are usually the most expensive part of any training run, and most teams can't keep them busy. The bottleneck usually isn't the model. It's getting data from where it lives to the GPU fast enough - and every second those chips sit waiting, you're burning both time and money. Today we're releasing the Unity Catalog Dataset (UCDataset) in Beta on AI Runtime. UCDataset is a native PyTorch data loader that streams Unity Catalog tables directly to every GPU in your training job, with no exports, no copies, and no custom loader code. On simulated production workloads, UCDataset cut training time by 10x compared with reading an exported Parquet copy of the same data. Most training data for your models already lives in Unity Catalog tables. Getting it into a distributed training job means picking one of three workarounds, and each one costs you time and money: Then there's the loader itself. Every GPU and every worker needs its own balanced slice of the data. Teams spend time building this by hand, and a subtle bug can mean the model trains on duplicated or skipped rows without anyone noticing. The result: expensive GPUs sit idle, training takes longer than it should, and ML engineers maintain data plumbing instead of improving models. UCDataset makes Unity Catalog tables a first-class data source for distributed PyTorch training. You describe what to read (a table, the columns you need, and a row filter) and UCDataset streams training-ready batches to every GPU. Benefits include: We benchmarked UCDataset on a simulated production workload, streaming a 300 GB feature table across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs to train a recommendation model and saw on average a 10x improvement in training time compared to loading data directly from Parquet. Say a team keeps user and item features with a click label stored in a main.recsys.ctr_features table. New impressions land on the table every day. story|title:agents are going async.content_excerpt: Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. story|title:gdpx measuring frontier mode.content_excerpt: GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin . Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0. Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes. The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely. It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. story|title:glassbrain read your agent s.content_excerpt: Know what your agent knows: open, diff and review the knowledge graphs agents write. Plain JSON in, one HTML file out. Your agent keeps knowledge graphs: of your code, your docs, its research, its own plans. glassbrain lets you read one at a glance, and when the agent learns something, shows you exactly what changed. parent says what sits inside what; that is the whole structure. Everything else is an edge. A JSON Schema describes every field, and the CLI answers in a form an agent can act on: Errors exit 1 ( --strict : warnings too), diff --exit-code exits 1 when anything changed, and --json gives the same as structured output. So an agent can build a graph in steps, validate each one, and check that a step did only its job. Not a pretty viewer: the widest channel from an agent's memory to your head. A few hundred nodes hold more than any report an agent could write you, and a picture of them is read in seconds: what is there, what sits inside what, what touches what. That only works if the picture holds still. Most graph viewers use a force layout: every edge pulls, so a few hundred relations decide the whole picture, and one change reshuffles all of it. glassbrain takes the shape from containment (folder ⊃ file ⊃ function, area ⊃ feature ⊃ step). Relations are drawn on top and move nothing. So the picture reads like a map, keeps reading at thousands of nodes, and stays where it was when the graph changes. Search ranks by how well a node matches, the detail panel renders the node's markdown, labels make room for each other instead of piling up, and dark mode is computed from the light palette. Graphs with layers can be stood up in 2.5D: The model already knows how. Codebase memory, docs knowledge bases, deep research, agent plans: each is a short skill or a single prompt. glassbrain does not build graphs; your agent does. Because the format is two arrays and the CLI checks every step, there is no extractor, pipeline or embedding store to build: the reach comes from the model, not from machinery around it. Every dataset in the demo was made that way by Claude Sonnet 5.5, and each has a RUN.md with the exact prompt and the token count. Already have a graph from another tool? Open it as it is; the format is detected from the content. Each tool's own notion of "inside" becomes the structure; everything else becomes edges. npx glassbrain convert <path> <out> writes any of them as plain glassbrain JSON ( formats ). Agent + npx. story|title:how we optimized browser use.content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. story|title:keep the agent s packets out.content_excerpt: Autonomous agents with shell access have superpowers, and a big attack surface. What this week’s Firecracker escape shows about VM boundaries, and how to set one that holds for tomorrow’s bug. An autonomous agent with a shell has superpowers. It installs packages, runs scripts, opens connections and fixes its own mistakes, without waiting for anyone. Nobody reviews each command. That’s the point. It’s also a big attack surface: every command it chooses, every package it pulls, every script a web page talks it into. So I run every agent in its own VM. This week, a guest VM got root on its host anyway. The first step was telling the host kernel where to write a checksum . The write-up , published on 7 November, targets Firecracker. I read it with one question: could this happen in Koala? Every network packet carries a checksum. Computing it costs CPU, so virtio lets the guest hand that job to the host: “the checksum starts here, write it there.” That shortcut is an offload , and it’s on by default in most fast VM networking. The kernel fix landed upstream on 14 October 2026. The bug gets patched. The pattern stays. The attack needs guest packets to reach the host kernel’s network stack with the hints attached. TAP and vhost-net, the usual fast paths, do exactly that. Koala uses neither. A virtio device and the guest agree on features at boot. Koala’s network device offers only two that reach the guest: a MAC address and modern virtio. No offloads, so the guest can’t even send the hints. That was true from day one. But a property nobody tests can disappear the day someone turns offloads on for speed. So now: The escape’s second step, hijacking the hypervisor, meets the second wall . Each VM’s Cloud Hypervisor runs as your user, under Landlock, seccomp and no_new_privs, and can’t open network sockets. To be honest about the limit: code that can already write host kernel memory doesn’t need the hypervisor, and no userspace sandbox stops it. What protects Koala here is the first wall. The sandbox is for the next bug. A boundary has to hold against tomorrow’s bug, not just today’s. And patch your host kernel anyway. Docker, or any VM tool that uses TAP, can still reach this one. For bulk data, that’s a real cost. Agents aren’t that workload. They call model APIs, fetch pages and clone repositories. story|title:memseal provenance containme.content_excerpt: MemSeal: a deterministic provenance-tracking containment layer on the write/recall boundary of AI agent long-term memory (GATE 2 self-reported FAIL; evaluation only). MemSeal is a containment layer on the write/recall boundary of an AI agent's long-term memory. Every memory entry is wrapped in a provenance envelope (who wrote it, from what source, derived from what, at which trust tier) inside a SHA-256 hash chain. Deterministic policies decide what may be stored, and a trust-tiered recall path decides what may be surfaced — especially before an external send or an irreversible action. Write policies: W1 quarantines instruction-form content from any source but the user; W2 makes derived entries inherit their worst ancestor's trust tier (no laundering a document into a "user fact"); W3 rejects cross-principal writes and filters cross-principal recall; W4 seals secrets (by entry_class=secret and by shape) so plaintext never lands in the store; W5 sends a fact that contradicts a sealed fact to review. The gate is judged on an independent holdout corpus authored by a separate party that never saw MemSeal's code, the dev corpus, or the reports. The bars are fixed in advance and never moved. Conditions: C0 raw store · C2 write path · C3 write + recall path · C4 + consolidation guard. Overall: GATE 2 = FAIL on v2. Three deterministic fixes between v1 and v2 (classification-based secret sealing; a sole-basis recall gate; consolidation root retirement) closed both security criteria — on v2, cross-principal + secret leaks went from 22 → 0 across C0 → C2, injection success 0.775 → 0.20 , and delayed-use 0.000 at C3. The two remaining failures are utility-side, and their causes are stated precisely (not hand-waved): Full detail, including an audit Errata that corrects earlier attribution wording, is in reports/phase2-regate.md and reports/phase2-fix.md . (The dev split shares the author's templates, so treat dev as an optimistic in-distribution reference; the independent holdout is the real test.) MemSeal was also run as a wrapper around Mem0 (fully local: Ollama LLM + Ollama embedder, in-memory vector store), 60 cases, two conditions: The real-LLM measurement harness is in memseal_phase2/ and talks only to a local Ollama ( qwen2.5:14b ). No external API, no API key, no network beyond localhost and the one-time model download. Tests use a mock LLM, so the suite runs without Ollama. story|title:new context engineering chal.content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. story|title:the components of agent memo.content_excerpt: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents. As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge. Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge. Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1). We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization. By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window). In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory. story|title:what is eval driven developm.content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. story|title:why agents are soon only goi.content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). story|title:why human insight is a strat.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. story|title:your experts have partners t.content_excerpt: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. story|variant:small|title:palette teachi.content_excerpt: Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Nobody makes a deck in one pass. story|variant:speech|title:a closer look.content_excerpt: Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.
